explanations.answer: His little daughter is near death
explanations.explanation: Jairus, a synagogue leader, puts it plainly: “My little daughter is near death.” That's why he's down at Jesus' feet, pleading urgently. I think a man in that spot has stopped caring who's watching. He just wants Jesus to come.

explanations.answer: His young son is sick with fever
explanations.explanation: Jairus says daughter, not son. Mark 5:23 has him say, “My little daughter is near death.” A fever never comes up in this passage at all. Easy to blur when you're reading fast, friend. I've grabbed the wrong tray in a hurry plenty of times myself.

explanations.answer: His servant is paralyzed in bed
explanations.explanation: Jairus is asking about his little daughter, and no servant shows up here. A paralyzed servant does appear in Matthew 8:5-6, but that's a centurion asking, a different man in a different story. In Mark 5:23 it's a father on his knees about his child.

Jairus says, “Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.” He asks for two things in one breath: that Jesus come, and that she live. Notice he doesn't ask for a speech or a plan. He asks Jesus to come.

This one is actually true. Jairus says, “Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.” He pleads for Jesus to come and lay His hands on her. That's the whole request, and it's right there in Mark 5:23.

The text says the opposite. Mark 5:26 tells us she had been under the care of many physicians and had spent all she had, “…but to no avail.” Then it adds that “…her condition had only grown worse.” Twelve years of this, and she was running low on everything.

Right, she didn't get better. She spent all she had on many physicians, and the text says, “…her condition had only grown worse.” That's a heavy part of her story. I think it's why what comes next hits so hard.
Mark 5:27 says she came up behind Him and touched His cloak. She doesn't announce herself or make a scene. She reaches out from behind in the middle of a pressing crowd, and that's all she does.

explanations.answer: She takes hold of His hand
explanations.explanation: Nobody grabs a hand here. The text says she came up behind Him and touched His cloak. It's a small touch from the back of the crowd, and it's the kind of detail I'd have missed in a rush too.
The text doesn't have her calling out. Mark 5:27 says she came up through the crowd behind Him and touched His cloak. Her moment is a quiet reach, not a shout.
She kept saying, “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” That's her own sentence from Mark 5:28. She wasn't just thinking it once, either. The text says she kept saying it.

Her words in Mark 5:28 were about healing: “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” Forgiveness isn't what she's saying. Twelve years of bleeding had left her needing a very different kind of help.

She never says anything about being noticed. Mark 5:28 gives her words: “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” Her words are all about healing, and I think a lot of people in that crowd would have been surprised by that.
Mark 5:29 says, “Immediately her bleeding stopped.” No waiting and no slow improvement. She also sensed in her body that she was healed, right there in the crowd.

explanations.answer: It slows over a few days
explanations.explanation: There's no slow fade here. Mark 5:29 says, “Immediately her bleeding stopped.” Not days and not weeks, but right then.

explanations.answer: It stops once she gets home
explanations.explanation: She doesn't have to go anywhere first. The bleeding stopped right when she touched His cloak, and the text says “Immediately.” She sensed it in her body on the spot, still standing in that crowd.

Jesus asks, “Who touched My garments?” He's aware that power has gone out from Him, and He turns to the crowd to ask. His question is about a touch. Out of all those people pressing in, one touch was different.
Jesus doesn't ask for a show of belief. Mark 5:30 has Him ask, “Who touched My garments?” His question points to one specific touch, not a vote from the crowd.

explanations.answer: Who is in need of healing
explanations.explanation: He asks about a touch, not about needs. In Mark 5:30 He turns to the crowd and says, “Who touched My garments?” If He'd asked who needed healing, I think half that crowd would have raised a hand.

The disciples don't point at anybody. They answer, “You can see the crowd pressing in on You, and yet You ask, ‘Who touched Me?’” They're looking at the whole crowd, not one person. Nobody has spotted her yet.
They don't point her out. Mark 5:31 has them say, “You can see the crowd pressing in on You, and yet You ask, ‘Who touched Me?’” To them it's a crowd, and that's all they see.
He doesn't let it go. Mark 5:32 says, “But He kept looking around to see who had done this.” The disciples answered, and He kept looking.
Right, He doesn't drop it. The text says, “But He kept looking around to see who had done this.” The disciples gave their answer, and Jesus kept looking around the crowd.

Mark 5:33 says she came, fell down before Him trembling in fear, and “told Him the whole truth.” She doesn't leave anything out. After twelve years of hiding her trouble, I think that took real nerve.
No name comes up in the text. Mark 5:33 says she told Him “the whole truth.” That's a lot more than a name.
The text doesn't say she apologized. It says she fell down before Him trembling in fear and “told Him the whole truth.” Whatever she said, she held nothing back.

No scolding anywhere. Jesus calls her “Daughter” and says, “Your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.” That's how He speaks to her in Mark 5:34, after she came forward trembling.
Right, no scolding. Mark 5:34 has Jesus say, “Daughter,” and then, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.” She came in fear, and she went out with peace.
Jesus says, “Daughter,” and then, “your faith has healed you.” That's Mark 5:34. He names her faith out loud, right in front of the crowd. Then He sends her off in peace, free of her affliction.
Jesus never mentions her strength. In Mark 5:34 He says, “your faith has healed you.” After twelve years of suffering, I'd guess her strength was running low, and He points to her faith instead.
Courage is a fair guess, since she came forward trembling. But Jesus says, “your faith has healed you” in Mark 5:34. Faith is the word He chose.

The messengers say it straight: “Your daughter is dead…” That's Mark 5:35, and it lands on Jairus while Jesus is still speaking to the woman. This is a heavy moment, and I think Jairus feels every word of it.
The news goes the other direction. The messengers tell him, “Your daughter is dead…” It's a hard moment in Mark 5:35, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: His daughter is asking for him
explanations.explanation: The messengers aren't carrying a request. Mark 5:35 has them say, “Your daughter is dead…” This is the heavy turn in the story, and it comes while Jesus is still speaking.

explanations.answer: Not to be afraid but just believe
explanations.explanation: Jesus overheard them and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe.” That's Mark 5:36. He speaks right to Jairus the moment the bad news lands. Short words for a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: To go home and wait for Him
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't send Jairus ahead or tell him to wait. In Mark 5:36 He says, “Do not be afraid; just believe.” Then they head to the house together.

explanations.answer: To call his family together to pray
explanations.explanation: That instruction isn't in the text. Mark 5:36 has Jesus say, “Do not be afraid; just believe.” That's the whole message He gives Jairus right then.
The text says otherwise. Mark 5:37 says He did not allow anyone to go with Him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. The crowd that had been pressing around Him stayed behind.
Right, no crowd. Mark 5:37 says He did not allow anyone to accompany Him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. Just three of His disciples go with Him to the house.

explanations.answer: She is not dead but asleep
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “The child is not dead, but asleep.” That's Mark 5:39, spoken right into all that weeping and wailing. He asks them first, “Why all this commotion and weeping?” Then He tells them what He says about the girl.

explanations.answer: She is gone beyond all help
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite of that. In Mark 5:39 He tells the people, “The child is not dead, but asleep.” He doesn't join the mourning.

explanations.answer: She will be healed by morning
explanations.explanation: No timeline from Jesus here. Mark 5:39 has Him say, “The child is not dead, but asleep.” He's speaking about her right now, in the middle of the commotion.

Mark 5:40 says, “And they laughed at Him.” Jesus had just said the child was not dead but asleep, and the people there laughed. It's a sad kind of laughter, I think, from people in the middle of grief.
Nobody's cheering in this scene. Mark 5:40 says, “And they laughed at Him.” The house was full of weeping and wailing, so a cheer would have been a big surprise.
The people were already loud with weeping and wailing, but the text says what they did when Jesus spoke: “And they laughed at Him.” That's Mark 5:40. The laughing comes right after His words.
Not so. Mark 5:40 says He put them all outside. Then He took the child's father and mother and His own companions, and went in to see the child. It's a small, quiet group.
Right, He clears the house. Jesus put them all outside, then took the child's father and mother and His own companions into the room. Nobody else gets to watch.

explanations.answer: Little girl I say to you get up
explanations.explanation: Mark 5:41 gives us the Aramaic and the meaning right together: “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” Jesus takes her by the hand and speaks directly to her. The writer even stops to translate it for us.

explanations.answer: Little girl rest now in peace
explanations.explanation: That's not what it means. Mark 5:41 says “Talitha koum!” means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” It's a command to rise, not to rest.

explanations.answer: Little girl your father is here
explanations.explanation: Her father is in the room, but that's not what the words say. Mark 5:41 tells us “Talitha koum!” means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” Jesus is speaking to her.
Mark 5:42 says, “Immediately the girl got up and began to walk around.” Jesus says get up, and she gets up. No slow start and no help needed.
This one is actually true. The text says, “Immediately the girl got up and began to walk around.” She doesn't just sit up, she walks around the room.

The writer tells us, “(she was twelve years old).” That's Mark 5:42, tucked in right as she starts walking around. Twelve also showed up earlier for the woman's years of bleeding, in Mark 5:25. Same number, two different stories running side by side.
The text says she was twelve. Mark 5:42 puts her age in a little aside as she walks around. Seven doesn't show up anywhere in this passage.
Close, but the text says twelve. In Mark 5:42 the writer adds, “(she was twelve years old).” Ten isn't in there, friend.

Mark 5:43 says Jesus “told them to give her something to eat.” After all that astonishment, there's a plain, practical instruction. I think it's a good reminder that I'd be the one standing there asking what's for dinner.
No trip to the synagogue is mentioned. Mark 5:43 says Jesus told them to give her something to eat. It's a simple instruction for after the miracle.
Nobody's told to let her sleep. She just got up and began to walk around, and Jesus told them to give her something to eat (Mark 5:42-43). That's the one more instruction in the text.
